entries.562c352fbbe97476bd4299c8e073ce4b1da93f25: <div sID="gen13082" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="135" osisID="Ps.135" sID="Ps.135"/> <div eID="gen13082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13083" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13084" type="x-p"/> This is one of the Hallelujah-psalms; that is the title of it, and that is the Amen of it, both its Alpha and its Omega. I. It begins with a call to praise God, particularly a call to the "servants of the Lord" to praise him, as in the foregoing psalm, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.1-Ps.135.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. It goes on to furnish us with matter for praise. God is to be praised, 1. As the God of Jacob, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.4">ver. 4</reference>. 2. As the God of gods, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.5">ver. 5</reference>. 3. As the God of the whole world, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.6-Ps.135.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. 4. As a terrible God to the enemies of Israel, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.8-Ps.135.11">ver. 8-11</reference>. 5. As a gracious God to Israel, both in what he had done for them and what he would do, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.12-Ps.135.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. 6. As the only living God, all other gods being vanity and a lie, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.15-Ps.135.18">ver. 15-18</reference>. III. It concludes with another exhortation to all persons concerned to praise God, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.19-Ps.135.21">ver. 19-21</reference>. In singing this psalm our hearts must be filled, as well as our mouths, with the high praises of God.
entries.c8694e67133cf71a7f9475ffc56ecaa068190ed9: <div eID="gen13084" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13083" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Majesty and Goodness of God.</title> <div sID="gen13085" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . Praise ye the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; praise <hi type="italic">him,</hi> O ye servants of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">2</hi> Ye that stand in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , in the courts of the house of our God, <hi type="super">3</hi> Praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> good: sing praises unto his name; for <hi type="italic">it is</hi> pleasant. <hi type="super">4</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath chosen Jacob unto himself, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Israel for his peculiar treasure. <div eID="gen13085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13086" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The duty we are called to—to <hi type="italic">praise the Lord,</hi> to <hi type="italic">praise his name; praise him,</hi> and again <hi type="italic">praise him.</hi> We must not only thank him for what he has done for us, but praise him for what he is in himself and has done for others; take all occasions to speak well of God and to give his truths and ways a good word. 2. The persons that are called upon to do this—the <hi type="italic">servants of the Lord,</hi> the priests and Levites <hi type="italic">that stand in his house,</hi> and all the devout and pious Israelites that stand <hi type="italic">in the courts of his house</hi> to worship there, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.2">v. 2</reference>. Those that have most reason to praise God who are admitted to the privileges of his house, and those see most reason who there behold his beauty and taste his bounty; from them it is expected, for to that end they enjoy their places. Who should praise him if they do not? 3. The reasons why we should praise God. (1.) Because he whom we are to praise <hi type="italic">is good,</hi> and goodness is that which every body will speak well of. He is good to all, and we must give him the praise of that. His goodness is his glory, and we must make mention of it to his glory. (2.) Because the work is its own wages: <hi type="italic">Sing praises to his name, for it is pleasant.</hi> It is best done with a cheerful spirit, and we shall have the pleasure of having done our duty. It is a heaven upon earth to be praising God; and the pleasure of that should quite put our mouths out of taste for the pleasures of sin. (3.) Because of the peculiar privileges of God's people (<reference osisRef="Ps.135.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord hath chosen Jacob to himself,</hi> and therefore Jacob is bound to praise him; for <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> God chose a people to himself that they might be unto him <hi type="italic">for a name and a praise</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.11">Jer. xiii. 11</reference>), and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> Jacob has abundant matter for praise, being thus dignified and distinguished. <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> is God's <hi type="italic">peculiar treasure</hi> above all people (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Exod. xix. 5</reference>); they are his <hi type="italic">Segullah,</hi> a people appropriated to him, and that he has a delight in, <hi type="italic">precious in his sight and honourable.</hi> For this distinguishing surprising favour, if the seed of Jacob do not praise him, they are the most unworthy ungrateful people under the sun.
entries.f42ff679504de38075ec15ae304b8c3a396ce792: <div eID="gen13086" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Majesty and Goodness of God.</title> <div sID="gen13087" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> For I know that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> great, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> our Lord <hi type="italic">is</hi> above all gods. <hi type="super">6</hi> Whatsoever the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> pleased, <hi type="italic">that</hi> did he in heaven, and in earth, in the seas, and all deep places. <hi type="super">7</hi> He causeth the vapours to ascend from the ends of the earth; he maketh lightnings for the rain; he bringeth the wind out of his treasuries. <hi type="super">8</hi> Who smote the firstborn of Egypt, both of man and beast. 9 <hi type="italic">Who</hi> sent tokens and wonders into the midst of thee, O Egypt, upon Pharaoh, and upon all his servants. <hi type="super">10</hi> Who smote great nations, and slew mighty kings; <hi type="super">11</hi> Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan: 12 And gave their land <hi type="italic">for</hi> a heritage, a heritage unto Israel his people. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thy name, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever; <hi type="italic">and</hi> thy memorial, O <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , throughout all generations. <hi type="super">14</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will judge his people, and he will repent himself concerning his servants. <div eID="gen13087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13088" type="x-p"/> The psalmist had suggested to us the goodness of God, as the proper matter of our cheerful praises; here he suggests to us the greatness of God as the proper matter of our awful praises; and on this he is most copious, because this we are less forward to consider. <div eID="gen13088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13089" type="x-p"/> I. He asserts the doctrine of God's greatness (<reference osisRef="Ps.135.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord is great,</hi> great indeed, who knows no limits of time or place. He asserts it with assurance, "I know that he is so; know it not only by observation of the proofs of it, but by belief of the revelation of it. I know it; I am sure of it; I know it by my own experience of the divine greatness working on my soul." He asserts it with a holy defiance of all pretenders, though they should join in confederacy against him. He is not only above any god, but above all gods, infinitely above them, between him and them there is no comparison. <div eID="gen13089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13090" type="x-p"/> II. He proves him to be a great God by the greatness of his power, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.6">v. 6</reference>. 1. He has an absolute power, and may do what he will: <hi type="italic">Whatsoever the Lord pleased, that did he,</hi> and none could control him, or say unto him, <hi type="italic">What doest thou?</hi> He does what he pleases, because he pleases, and gives not an account of any of his matters. 2. He has an almighty power and can do what he will; if he will work, none shall hinder. 3. This absolute almighty power is of universal extent; he does what he will <hi type="italic">in heaven, in earth, in the seas,</hi> and in <hi type="italic">all the deep places</hi> that are in the bottom of the sea or the bowels of the earth. The gods of the heathen can do nothing; but our God can do any thing and does do every thing. <div eID="gen13090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13091" type="x-p"/> III. He gives instances of his great power, <div eID="gen13091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13092" type="x-p"/> 1. In the kingdom of nature, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.7">v. 7</reference>. All the powers of nature prove the greatness of the God of nature, from whom they are derived and on whom they depend. The chain of natural causes was not only framed by him at first, but is still preserved by him. (1.) It is by his power that exhalations are drawn up from the terraqueous globe. The heat of the sun raises them, but it has that power from God, and therefore it is given as an instance of the glory of God that <hi type="italic">nothing is hidden from the heat</hi> of the sun, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.6">Ps. xix. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">He causes the vapours to ascend</hi> (not only unhelped, but unseen, by us) from the earth, <hi type="italic">from the ends of the earth,</hi> that is, from the seas, by which the earth is surrounded. (2.) It is he who, out of those vapours so raised, forms the rain, so that the earth is no loser by the vapours it sends up, for they are returned with advantage in fruitful showers. (3.) Out of the same vapours (such is his wonderful power) he <hi type="italic">makes lightnings or the rain;</hi> by them he opens the bottles of heaven, and shakes the clouds, that they may water the earth. Here are fire and water thoroughly reconciled by divine omnipotence. They come together, and yet the water does not quench the fire, nor the fire lick up the water, as fire from heaven did when God pleased, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.38">1 Kings xviii. 38</reference>. (4.) The same exhalations, to serve another purpose, are converted into winds, which blow where they list, from what point of the compass they will, and we are so far from directing them that we cannot tell whence they come nor whither they go, but God <hi type="italic">brings them out of his treasuries</hi> with as much exactness and design as a prudent prince orders money to issue out of his exchequer. <div eID="gen13092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13093" type="x-p"/> 2. In the kingdoms of men; and here he mentions the great things God had formerly done for his people Israel, which were proofs of God's greatness as well as of his goodness, and confirmations of the truth of the scriptures of the Old Testament, which began to be written by Moses, the person employed in working those miracles. Observe God's sovereign dominion and irresistible power, (1.) In bringing Israel out of Egypt, humbling Pharaoh by many plagues, and so forcing him to let them go. These plagues are called <hi type="italic">tokens</hi> and <hi type="italic">wonders,</hi> because they came not in the common course of providence, but there was something miraculous in each of them. They were <hi type="italic">sent upon Pharaoh and all his servants,</hi> his subjects; but the Israelites, whom God claimed for his servants, his son, his first-born, his free-born, were exempted from them, and no plague came nigh their dwelling. The death of the first-born both of men and cattle was the heaviest of all the plagues, and that which gained the point. (2.) In destroying the kingdoms of Canaan before them, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.10">v. 10</reference>. Those that were in possession of the land designed for Israel had all possible advantages for keeping possession. The people were numerous, and warlike, and confederate against Israel. They were great nations. Yet, if a great nation has a meek and mean-spirited prince, it lies exposed; but these great nations had <hi type="italic">mighty kings,</hi> and yet they were all smitten and slain—<hi type="italic">Sihon</hi> and <hi type="italic">Og,</hi> and <hi type="italic">all the kingdoms of Canaan,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.135.10-Ps.135.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. No power of hell or earth can prevent the accomplishment of the promise of God when the time, the set time, for it has come. (3.) In settling them in the land of promise. He that gives kingdoms to whomsoever he pleases gave Canaan to be a heritage to Israel his people. It came to them by inheritance, for their ancestors had the promise of it, though not the possession; and it descended as an inheritance to their seed. This was done long before, yet God is now praised for it; and with good reason, for the children were now enjoying the benefit of it. <div eID="gen13093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13094" type="x-p"/> IV. He triumphs in the perpetuity of God's glory and grace. 1. Of his glory (<reference osisRef="Ps.135.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy name, O God! endures for ever.</hi> God's manifestations of himself to his people have everlasting fruits and consequences. <hi type="italic">What God doeth it shall be for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.14">Eccl. iii. 14</reference>. His name endures for ever in the constant and everlasting praises of his people; his memorial endures, has endured hitherto, and shall still endure throughout all generations of the church. This seems to refer to <reference osisRef="Exod.3.15">Exod. iii. 15</reference>, where, when God had called himself <hi type="italic">the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,</hi> he adds, <hi type="italic">This is my name for ever and this is my memorial unto all generations.</hi> God is, and will be, always the same to his church, a gracious, faithful, wonder-working God; and his church is, and will be, the same to him, a thankful praising people; and thus his name <hi type="italic">endures for ever.</hi> 2. Of his grace. He will be kind to his people. (1.) He will plead their cause against others that contend with them. <hi type="italic">He will judge his people,</hi> that is, he will judge for them, and will not suffer them to be run down. (2.) He will not himself contend for ever with them, but will <hi type="italic">repent himself concerning his servants,</hi> and not proceed in his controversy with them; he will be entreated for them, or he will be comforted concerning them; he will return in ways of mercy to them and will delight to do them good. <reference osisRef="Ps.135.14">This verse</reference> is taken from the song of Moses, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.36">Deut. xxxii. 36</reference>.
entries.9bbd986ef805aa4275c50225ba75cd73b7d4842a: <div eID="gen13094" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">An Invitation to Praise.</title> <div sID="gen13095" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> The idols of the heathen <hi type="italic">are</hi> silver and gold, the work of men's hands. <hi type="super">16</hi> They have mouths, but they speak not; eyes have they, but they see not; <hi type="super">17</hi> They have ears, but they hear not; neither is there <hi type="italic">any</hi> breath in their mouths. <hi type="super">18</hi> They that make them are like unto them: <hi type="italic">so is</hi> every one that trusteth in them. <hi type="super">19</hi> Bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O house of Israel: bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O house of Aaron: <hi type="super">20</hi> Bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O house of Levi: ye that fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">21</hi> Blessed be the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> out of Zion, which dwelleth at Jerusalem. Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen13095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13096" type="x-p"/> The design of these verses is, <div eID="gen13096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13097" type="x-p"/> I. To arm the people of God against idolatry and all false worship, by showing what sort of gods they were that the heathen worshipped, as we had it before, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.4-Ps.115.8">Ps. cxv. 4</reference>, &c. 1. They were gods of their own making; being so, they could have no power but what their makers gave them, and then what power could their makers receive from them? The images were the <hi type="italic">work of men's hands,</hi> and the deities that were supposed to inform them were as much the creatures of men's fancy and imagination. 2. They had the shape of animals, but could not perform the least act, no, not of the <hi type="italic">animal</hi> life. They could neither <hi type="italic">see,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">hear,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">speak,</hi> nor so much as <hi type="italic">breathe;</hi> and therefore to make them with <hi type="italic">eyes,</hi> and <hi type="italic">ears,</hi> and <hi type="italic">mouths,</hi> and <hi type="italic">nostrils,</hi> was such a jest that one would wonder how reasonable creatures could suffer themselves to be so imposed upon as to expect any good from such mock-deities. 3. Their worshippers were therefore as stupid and senseless as they were, both those that made them to be worshipped and those that trusted in them when they were made, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.18">v. 18</reference>. The worshipping of such gods as were the objects of sense, and senseless, made the worshippers sensual and senseless. Let our worshipping a God that is a Spirit make us spiritual and wise. <div eID="gen13097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13098" type="x-p"/> II. To stir up the people of God to true devotion in the worship of the true God, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.19-Ps.135.21">v. 19-21</reference>. The more deplorable the condition of the Gentile nations that worship idols is the more are we bound to thank God that we know better. Therefore, 1. Let us set ourselves about the acts of devotion, and employ ourselves in them: <hi type="italic">Bless the Lord,</hi> and again and again, <hi type="italic">bless the Lord.</hi> In the parallel place (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.9-Ps.115.11">Ps. cxv. 9-11</reference>), by way of inference from the impotency of idols, the duty thus pressed upon us is to <hi type="italic">trust in the Lord;</hi> here to <hi type="italic">bless him;</hi> by putting our trust in God we give glory to him, and those that depend upon God shall not want matter of thanksgiving to him. All persons that knew God are here called to praise him—the <hi type="italic">house of Israel</hi> (the nation in general), the <hi type="italic">house of Aaron</hi> and the <hi type="italic">house of Levi</hi> (the Lord's ministers that attended in his sanctuary), and all others <hi type="italic">that feared the Lord,</hi> though they were not of the house of Israel. 2. Let God have the glory of all: <hi type="italic">Blessed be the Lord.</hi> The tribute of praise arises <hi type="italic">out of Zion.</hi> All God's works do praise him, but his saints bless him; and they need not go far to pay their tribute, for he <hi type="italic">dwells in Jerusalem,</hi> in his church, which they are members of, so that he is always nigh unto them to receive their homage. The condescensions of his grace, in dwelling with men upon the earth, call for our grateful and thankful returns, and our repeated Hallelujahs.  <chapter eID="Ps.135"/> <div eID="gen13098" type="x-p"/>

entries.b21dba2b3003a2c0c1d636b30a9030e0750e188e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7052"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 135</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.135.1-Ps.135.21">Psa 135:1-21</reference>. A Psalm of praise, in which God's relations to His Church, His power in the natural world, and in delivering His people, are contrasted with the vanity of idols and idol-worship.</title> <div sID="gen10821" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7052"/>1-3. In the general call for praise, the priests, that stand in the house of the Lord, are specially mentioned. <div eID="gen10821" type="x-p"/>
entries.a0dc82f1e8b0d1501b653ad503a48b4a4396ee58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7053"/><div sID="gen10822" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7053"/>4-7. God's choice of Israel is the first reason assigned for rendering praise; the next, His manifested greatness in creation and providence. <div eID="gen10822" type="x-p"/>
entries.2596a2cec3336d61b6f045ef09b9faebef90a40b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7055"/><div sID="gen10824" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7055"/>8-9. The last plague [Ex 12:29] is cited to illustrate His "tokens and wonders." <div eID="gen10824" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b7d6c7af0ec27c20ce606e05deaca383464cbd8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7056"/><div sID="gen10825" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7056"/>10-12. The conquest of Canaan was by God's power, not that of the people. <div eID="gen10825" type="x-p"/>
entries.15db1840f7e14d787d79306f80edcf79d1572bfe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7057"/><div sID="gen10826" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7057"/><hi type="bold">13. heritage--</hi>or, "possession."<div eID="gen10826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10827" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">name ... memorial--</hi>Each denote that by which God is made known. <div eID="gen10827" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1c0a2c8857782716e13e33bd245ae7449abf343: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7058"/><div sID="gen10828" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7058"/><hi type="bold">14. will judge--</hi>do justice (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.2">Psa 72:2</reference>).<div eID="gen10828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10829" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">repent himself--</hi>change His dealings (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.13">Psa 90:13</reference>). <div eID="gen10829" type="x-p"/>
entries.ddf05772584f7b5830ae49ef05729e93183ba9b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7059"/><div sID="gen10830" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7059"/>15-18. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.115.4-Ps.115.8">Psa 115:4-8</reference>). <div eID="gen10830" type="x-p"/>
entries.58b47e052fe80c2c570a8032dc8e4afa7f63be8c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7061"/><div sID="gen10832" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7061"/>19-21. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.115.9-Ps.115.11">Psa 115:9-11</reference>). There we have "trust" for "bless" here. <div eID="gen10832" type="x-p"/>

entries.8bd4fb90711655c04771660ff0c5d1b51d629675: <div eID="gen23225" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23226" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23227" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23227" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23226" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23228" type="x-p"/> An exhortation to praise God for his goodness and greatness, <reference osisRef="Psa.135.1-Psa.135.5">Psa 135:1-5</reference>; for his wonders in nature, <reference osisRef="Psa.135.6">Psa 135:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.135.7">Psa 135:7</reference>; his wonders done in Egypt, <reference osisRef="Psa.135.8">Psa 135:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.135.9">Psa 135:9</reference>; in the wilderness, <reference osisRef="Psa.135.10-Psa.135.12">Psa 135:10-12</reference>; for his goodness to his people, <reference osisRef="Psa.135.13">Psa 135:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.135.14">Psa 135:14</reference>. The vanity of idols, <reference osisRef="Psa.135.15-Psa.135.18">Psa 135:15-18</reference>. Israel, with its priests and Levites, exhorted to praise the Lord, <reference osisRef="Psa.135.19-Psa.135.21">Psa 135:19-21</reference>. <div eID="gen23228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23229" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is intimately connected with the preceding. It is an exhortation addressed to the priests and Levites, and to all Israel, to publish the praises of the Lord. The conclusion of this Psalm is nearly the same with Psalm 115; and what is said about idols, and the effects of the power of God, seems to be taken from it and the tenth chapter of Jeremiah; and from these and other circumstances it appears the Psalm was written after the captivity; and might as Calmet conjectures, have been used at the dedication of the second temple. <div eID="gen23229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23230" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23231" type="x-p"/> Praise ye the Lord - This may be considered as the title, for it has none other. <div eID="gen23231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23232" type="x-p"/> Praise ye the name of the Lord - Perhaps the original הללו את שם יהוה haleu eth shem Yehovah, should be translated, Praise ye the name Jehovah; that is, Praise God in his infinite essence of being, holiness, goodness, and truth.
entries.60a13f2cc97d0d1caa5f5af9e7e7cce324fed9b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23233" type="x-p"/> Ye that stand - Priests and Levites. For which he gives several reasons.
entries.20284f4c752c1b6764aea9bd623e7a36d7c32cc5: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23234" type="x-p"/> The Lord is good - Here is the first reason why he should be praised; and a second is subjoined: <div eID="gen23234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23235" type="x-p"/> For it is pleasant - It is becoming to acknowledge this infinite Being, and our dependence on him; and it is truly comfortable to an upright mind to be thus employed.
entries.1fc28757e18bb69529bcbccda909680f277173d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23236" type="x-p"/> For the Lord hath chosen Jacob - This is a third reason. He has taken the Israelites for his peculiar people, סגלתו segullatho, his peculiar treasure; and now has brought them home to himself from their captivity and wanderings.
entries.c7193a670884497676ef5d9e23066dca656fb3fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23237" type="x-p"/> The Lord is great - Unlimited in his power: another reason. <div eID="gen23237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23238" type="x-p"/> Is above all gods - Every class of being, whether idolized or not; because he is the Fountain of existence. This is a fifth reason.
entries.4a5c98cf018181952e0c8235beea16e59760ed52: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23239" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever the Lord pleased - All that he has done is right, and therefore it is pleasing in his sight. He is the author of all existence. Angels, men, spirits, the heavens, the earth, and all their contents, were made by him, and are under his control.
entries.56db28a9cfaea352effe1eccd5c714fa3b2b3dce: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23240" type="x-p"/> He causeth the vapours to ascend - Dr. Shaw thinks that the account here refers to the autumnal rains in the east. Of them he speaks as follows: "Seldom a night passes without much lightning in the north-west quarter, but not attended with thunder; and when this lightning appears in the west or south-west points, it is a sure sign of the approaching rain, which is often followed by thunder. A squall of wind and clouds of dust are the sure forerunners of the first rain." This account induces Mr. Harmer to believe that the word נשאים nesiim, should be translated clouds, not vapours. It shows that God: - <div eID="gen23240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23241" type="x-p"/> Maketh lightnings for the rain - The squalls of wind bring on these refreshing showers, and are therefore precious things of the treasuries of God, and when he thunders, it is the noise of waters in the heavens. See <reference osisRef="Jer.10.13">Jer 10:13</reference>, which contains almost the same words as those in this verse: "When he uttereth his voice, there is a multitude of waters in the heavens; and he causeth the vapours to ascend from the ends of the earth; he maketh lightnings with rain, and bringeth forth the wind out of his treasuries."
entries.285c8564094acc304c74b4259a012ccbade49d29: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23242" type="x-p"/> Who smote the first-born of Egypt - See the parallel passages.
entries.f2fcc99d0614f427d5e9409acfb6fb127552f369: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen23242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23243" type="x-p"/> The Lord will judge his people - He will do them justice against their enemies.
entries.e24bd7157dfd7e61b362ced6832fc1e122192657: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen23243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23244" type="x-p"/> The idols of the heathen - This verse and the following, to the end of the 18th, are almost word for word the same as <reference osisRef="Psa.115.4-Psa.115.8">Psa 115:4-8</reference> (note), where see the notes.
entries.5d7b97765004d58608f9fbf90108fb4aaf4e7245: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen23244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23245" type="x-p"/> To this verse one of Kennicott's MSS. adds the <reference osisRef="Psa.115.6">Psa 115:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Psa.115.7">Psa 115:7</reference> of Psalm 115.
entries.a65e9fae488e09c41f944888cc3f03fe6ccd5832: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen23245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23246" type="x-p"/> Bless the Lord. O house, etc. - See similar verses, <reference osisRef="Psa.115.9-Psa.115.13">Psa 115:9-13</reference> (note), and the notes there.
entries.6884f43099a3cd89672d173c3a19788c309084da: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen23246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23247" type="x-p"/> Blessed be the Lord out of Zion - Who has once more restored our temple and city, and now condescends to dwell with us in Jerusalem.  <chapter eID="Ps.135"/> <div eID="gen23247" type="x-p"/>

entries.fd253491fe92746946a183c7f64ceb34258b0904: <div eID="gen10243" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Four-Voiced Hallelujah to the God of Israel, the God of Gods</title> <div sID="gen10244" type="x-p"/> Psalms 135 is here and there (vid., <hi type="italic">Tôsefôth Pesachim</hi> 117 <hi type="italic">a</hi>) taken together with <reference osisRef="Ps.134.1-Ps.134.3">Psa 134:1-3</reference> as one Psalm. The combining of Ps 115 with <reference osisRef="Ps.114.1-Ps.114.8">Psa 114:1-8</reference> is a misapprehension caused by the inscriptionless character of Ps 115, whereas Ps 135 and <reference osisRef="Ps.134.1-Ps.134.3">Psa 134:1-3</reference> certainly stand in connection with one another. For the Hallelujah Psalms 135 is, as the mutual relation between the beginning and close of <reference osisRef="Ps.134.1-Ps.134.3">Psa 134:1-3</reference> shows, a Psalm-song expanded out of this shorter hymn, that is in part drawn from Ps 115. <div eID="gen10244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10245" type="x-p"/> It is a Psalm in the mosaic style. Even the Latin poet Lucilius transfers the figure of mosaic-work to style, when he says: <hi type="italic">quam lepide lexeis compostae ut tesserulae omnes...</hi> In the case of Psalms 135 it is not the first time that we have met with this kind of style. We have already had a glimpse of it in <reference osisRef="Ps.97.1-Ps.97.12">Psa 97:1-12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.98.1">Psa 98:1</reference>-9. These Psalms were composed more especially of deutero-Isaianic passages, whereas Psalms 135 takes its <hi type="italic">tesserulae</hi> out of the Law, Prophets, and Psalms.
entries.5c4a2f5bd39dbff5d3b0a7d8f683279607b4f875: <reference osisRef="Ps.135.1-Ps.135.4">Psa 135:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen10245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10246" type="x-p"/> The beginning is taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.134.1">Psa 134:1</reference>; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.135.2">Psa 135:2</reference></hi> recalls <reference osisRef="Ps.116.19">Psa 116:19</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.92.14">Psa 92:14</reference>); and <reference osisRef="Ps.135.4">Psa 135:4</reference> is an echo of Deu 7:6. The servants of Jahve to whom the summons is addressed, are not, as in Psa 134:1., His official servants in particular, but according to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.135.2">Psa 135:2</reference></hi>, where the courts, in the plural, are allotted to them as their standing-place, and according to <reference osisRef="Ps.135.19-Ps.135.20">Psa 135:19-20</reference>, those who fear Him as a body. The threefold <hi type="italic">Jahve</hi> at the beginning is then repeated in <hi type="italic">Jāh</hi> (הללוּ־יהּ, cf. note 1 to PsPsa 104:35), <hi type="italic">Jahve</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Jāh</hi>. The subject of כּי נעים is by no means Jahve (Hupfeld), whom they did not dare to call נעים in the Old Testament, but either the Name, according to Ps 54:8 (Luther, Hitzig), or, which is favoured by <reference osisRef="Ps.147.1">Psa 147:1</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.22.18">Pro 22:18</reference>), the praising of His Name (Appolinaris: ἐπεὶ τόδε καλὸν ἀείδειν): His Name to praise is a delightful employ, which is incumbent on Israel as the people of His choice and of His possession.
entries.2d61fdf303c2df96dbd52ab48a845f723de661bd: <reference osisRef="Ps.135.5-Ps.135.7">Psa 135:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen10246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10247" type="x-p"/> The praise itself now begins. כּי in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.135.4">Psa 135:4</reference></hi> set forth the ground of the pleasant duty, and the כי that begins this strophe confirms that which warrants the summons out of the riches of the material existing for such a hymn of praise. Worthy is He to be praised, for Israel knows full well that He who hath chosen it is the God of gods. The beginning is taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.115.3">Psa 115:3</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ps.135.7">Psa 135:7</reference> from <reference osisRef="Jer.10.13">Jer 10:13</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.16">Psa 51:16</reference>). Heaven, earth, and water are the three kingdoms of created things, as in Exo 20:4. נשׂיא signifies that which is lifted up, ascended; here, as in Jeremiah, a cloud. The meaning of בּרקים למּטר עשׂה is not: He makes lightnings into rain, i.e., resolves them as it were into rain, which is unnatural; but either according to Zec 10:1 : He produces lightnings in behalf of rain, in order that the rain may pour down in consequence of the thunder and lightning, or poetically: He makes lightnings for the rain, so that the rain is announced (Apollinaris) and accompanied by them. Instead of מוצא (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.78.16">Psa 78:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.105.43">Psa 105:43</reference>), which does not admit of the retreating of the tone, the expression is מוצא, the ground-form of the <hi type="italic">part.</hi> <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. for plurals like מחצרים, מחלמים, מעזרים, perhaps not without being influenced by the ויּוצא in Jeremiah, for it is not מוצא from מצא that signifies “producing,” but מוציא = מפיק. The metaphor of the treasuries is like Job 38:22. What is intended is the fulness of divine power, in which lie the grounds of the origin and the impulses of all things in nature.
entries.900e8b21f1f4269cdc6074523ffc4aca448707c9: <reference osisRef="Ps.135.8-Ps.135.9">Psa 135:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen10247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10248" type="x-p"/> Worthy is He to be praised, for He is the Redeemer out of Egypt. בּתוככי as in <reference osisRef="Ps.116.19">Psa 116:19</reference>, cf. Psa 105:27.
entries.59932e3df6e4e59569e30f680c01789a3697387f: <reference osisRef="Ps.135.10-Ps.135.12">Psa 135:10-12</reference> <div eID="gen10248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10249" type="x-p"/> Worthy is He to be praised, for He is the Conqueror of the Land of Promise. in connection with <reference osisRef="Ps.135.10">Psa 135:10</reference> one is reminded of <reference osisRef="Deut.4.38">Deu 4:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.1">Deu 7:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.1">Deu 9:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.23">Deu 11:23</reference>; Jos 23:9. גּוים רבּים are here not many, but great peoples (cf. גּדלים in <reference osisRef="Ps.136.17">Psa 136:17</reference>), since the parallel word עצוּמים is by no means intended of a powerful number, but of powerful might (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Isa 53:12</reference>). As to the rest also, the poet follows the Book of Deuteronomy: viz., לכל ממלכות as in <reference osisRef="Deut.3.21">Deu 3:21</reference>, and נתן נחלה as in <reference osisRef="Deut.4.38">Deu 4:38</reference> and other passages. It is all Deuteronomic with the exception of the שׁ, and the ל e in <reference osisRef="Ps.135.11">Psa 135:11</reference> as the <hi type="italic">nota accus.</hi> (as in Psa 136:19., cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.69.6">Psa 69:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">Psa 116:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.129.3">Psa 129:3</reference>); the construction of הרג is just as Aramaizing in <reference osisRef="Job.5.2">Job 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.30">2Sa 3:30</reference> (where <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.30-2Sam.3.31">2Sa 3:30-31</reference>, like <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.36-2Sam.3.37">2Sa 3:36-37</reference>, are a later explanatory addition). The הרג alternating with הכּה is, next to the two kings, also referred to the kingdoms of Canaan, viz., their inhabitants. Og was also an Amoritish king, Deu 3:8.
entries.5c5a3ad49e967738cdeb1e0ba9ec53ffea355212: <reference osisRef="Ps.135.13-Ps.135.14">Psa 135:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen10249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10250" type="x-p"/> This God who rules so praiseworthily in the universe and in the history of Israel is the same yesterday, and to-day, and for ever. Just as <reference osisRef="Ps.135.13">Psa 135:13</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.102.13">Psa 102:13</reference>) is taken from <reference osisRef="Exod.3.15">Exo 3:15</reference>, so <reference osisRef="Ps.135.14">Psa 135:14</reference> is taken from <reference osisRef="Deut.32.36">Deu 32:36</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.90.13">Psa 90:13</reference>, and vid., on <reference osisRef="Heb.10.30">Heb 10:30</reference>-31.
entries.f77c113c3e50c08cf04537cef145905f8c64baed: <reference osisRef="Ps.135.15-Ps.135.18">Psa 135:15-18</reference> <div eID="gen10250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10251" type="x-p"/> For the good of His proved church He ever proves Himself to be the Living God, whereas idols and idol-worshippers are vain - throughout following <reference osisRef="Ps.115.4-Ps.115.8">Psa 115:4-8</reference>, but with some abridgments. Here only the אף used as a particle recalls what is said there of the organ of smell (אף) of the idols that smells not, just as the רוּח which is here (as in <reference osisRef="Jer.10.14">Jer 10:14</reference>) denied to the idols recalls the הריח denied to them there. It is to be rendered: also there is not a being of breath, i.e., there is no breath at all, not a trace thereof, in their mouth. It is different in <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.9">1Sa 21:9</reference>, where אין ישׁ (not אין) is meant to be equivalent to the Aramaic אין אית, <hi type="italic">num</hi> (<hi type="italic">an</hi>) <hi type="italic">est</hi>; אין is North-Palestinian, and equivalent to the interrogatory אם (after which the Targum renders אלּוּ אית).
entries.e10c313949ff397ced25074a556de50c3e47c0c3: <reference osisRef="Ps.135.19-Ps.135.21">Psa 135:19-21</reference> <div eID="gen10251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10252" type="x-p"/> A call to the praise of Jahve, who is exalted above the gods of the nations, addressed to Israel as a whole, rounds off the Psalm by recurring to its beginning. The threefold call in <reference osisRef="Ps.115.9-Ps.115.11">Psa 115:9-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.2-Ps.118.4">Psa 118:2-4</reference>, is rendered fourfold here by the introduction of the house of the Levites, and the wishing of a blessing in <reference osisRef="Ps.134.3">Psa 134:3</reference> is turned into an ascription of praise. Zion, whence Jahve’s self-attestation, so rich in power and loving-kindness, is spread abroad, is also to be the place whence His glorious attestation by the mouth of men is spread abroad. History has realized this.  <chapter eID="Ps.135"/> <div eID="gen10252" type="x-p"/>

entries.53a883bf858e45262c396c0f971b5febc97e7c69:
Psalm 135
An exhortation to praise God, both for his goodness specially shown to his chosen people, and for his power and glory apparent in the world at large. A contrast is drawn between idols, which had but a vain show of divinity, and the God of Israel, who had established his claim to be considered the only true God by clear and indubitable proofs, and this with the view of leading his people the more cheerfully to praise him, and submit to his government.
Halleluiah.
Psalm 135:1-4
1. Praise ye the name of Jehovah,
“Perhaps the original, הללו שם יהוה, halelu et shem Jehovah, should be translated, Praise ye the namee Jehovah: that is, praise God in his infinite essence, of being, holiness, goodness, and truth.”—Dr. Adam Clarke.
praise him, O ye servants of Jehovah! 2. Ye who stand in the house of Jehovah, and ye who stand in the courts of the house of our God.
The words ye who stand we have supplied in the second clause, as being necessary to bring out the sense which Calvin attaches to it. The בית יהוה “the house of Jehovah,” mentioned in the first clause, remarks Men-dlessohn in his Beor, is the place where the priests stood; whilst “the courts” surrounding the temple, referred to in the second clause, were occupied by the people when engaged in their public prayers.
3. Praise God, for good is Jehovah: sing unto his name, for it is pleasant. 4. For God hath chosen Jacob
The name “Jacob” is here put by metonymy for the posterity of Jacob, as is evident from the parallelism of the two members.
unto himself, and Israel for his peculiar treasure.
 
1. Praise ye the name of Jehovah Though this Psalm begins almost in the same manner with the preceding, the Psalmist would not appear to be addressing the Levites exclusively, but the people generally, since the reasons given for praising God are equally applicable to all God’s children. No mention is made of night watching, or of their standing constantly in the Temple. But indeed, as it was the special duty of the priests to take the lead in this devotional exercise, to give out, if we might use such an expression, and sing the praises of God before the people, there is no reason why we should not suppose that they are primarily addressed, and stirred up to their duty. We need only to examine the ‘words more closely in order to be convinced that the people are included as next in order to the priests.
“Et quand on advisera de bien pres aux mots, on y trouvera que le peuple est adjoint, etc.”—Fr.
For the Psalmist addresses the servants of God who stand in the temple, then those who are in the courts, whereas no notice was taken of the courts in the former Psalm. Mention seems to be made of courts in the plural number, because the priests had their court; and then there was another common to all the people, for by the law spoken of, (Leviticus 16:17,) they were prohibited from entering the sanctuary. To prevent any feeling of disgust which might arise from the very frequent repetition of this exhortation to the praises of God, it is only necessary to remember, as was already observed, that there is no sacrifice in which he takes greater delight than the expression of our gratitude. Thus, (Psalm 50:14,)
“Sacrifice unto the Lord thanksgiving, and pay your vows to the Most High;”
and, (Psalm 116:12, 13,)
“What shal1 I render unto the Lord for all his benefits? I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the Lord.”
Particular attention is to be paid to those passages of Scripture which speak in such high terms of that worship of God which is spiritual; otherwise we may be led, in the exercise of a misguided zeal, to spend our labor upon trifles, and in this respect imitate the example of too many who have wearied themselves with ridiculous attempts to invent additions to the service of God, while they have neglected what is of all other things most important. This is the reason why the Holy Spirit so repeatedly inculcates the duty of praise. It is that we may not undervalue, or grow careless in this devotional exercise. It implies, too, an indirect censure of our tardiness in proceeding to the duty, for he would not reiterate the admonition were we ready and active in the discharge of it. The expression in the end of the verse — because it is sweet, admits of two meanings — that the name of God is sweet, as in the previous clause it was said that God is good — or, that it is a sweet and pleasant thing to sing’ God’s praises. The Hebrew word נעים naim, properly signifies beautiful or comely, and this general signification answers best.
“Signifie proprement chose bien seante ou belle: et ce sens general convient mieux.” — Fr.

                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXXXV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>This Psalm contains an exhortation to all the Israelites, and especially to the Priests and Levites, to praise God for his great and wonderful works; some particulars whereof are here recorded.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 PRaise ye the LORD, praise ye the name of the LORD, praise him, O ye servants of the LORD <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Ye Priests and Levites, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 134. 1.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Ye that stand in the house of the LORD, in the courts <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Either in the Temple or the inner Court, which were appropriated to the Priests and Levites; or in the outward Court, which was for the people. See 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 4. 9.</ns0:note> of the house of our God.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Praise ye the LORD, for the LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> good <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Bountiful and gracious, especially to you, and therefore he justly expects and deserves your praises.</ns0:note>: sing <ns0:hi>praises</ns0:hi> unto his name, for <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sant <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The work it self of singing praises to God is pleasant, as it is more fully expressed, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 147. 1.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 19. 5. Deut. 7. 6.</ns0:note> the LORD hath chosen Jacob for himself, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> Israel for his peculiar treasure.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 For I know that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 95. 3.</ns0:note> the LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> great, and <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> our LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> above all gods <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Above all that are called <ns0:hi>Gods,</ns0:hi> or worshipped as Gods by the heathen people. And therefore seeing they com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monly praise and extol their Idols, it becometh you not to be silent as to the praises of your God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 115. 3.</ns0:note> Whatsoever the LORD pleased <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either in the creation or government of them.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> did he in heaven and in earth <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">His power and juri<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                  <ns0:p n="8">8 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 12. 12, 29.</ns0:note> Who smote the first-born <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">From the general works of Nature he comes to Gods special works of Providence towards his people.</ns0:note> of Egypt, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">

                  <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:hi>Who</ns0:hi> sent tokens and wonders into the midst of thee, O Egypt, upon Pharaoh, and upon all his servants.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:512" />10 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Numb. 21. 24, 25, 26, 34, 35.</ns0:note> Who smote great nations, and slew mighty kings.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Sihon king of the Amorite, and Og king of Bashan, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Josh. 12. 7.</ns0:note> all the kingdoms of Canaan.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Josh. 12. 7. Psal. 78. 55.</ns0:note> And gave their land <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> an heritage, an heritage unto Israel his people.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Thy <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 102. 12.</ns0:note> name, O LORD, <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> thy memorial, O LORD, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ration and ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neration.</ns0:note> throughout all generations <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">These wonderful works of thine shall never be forgotten.                   <ns0:p n="14">14 For the LORD will judge his people <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Will in due time plead the cause of his people, or give judgment for them, as this phrase is used <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 32. 36. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 5. 28 & 22. 16.</ns0:note>, and he will repent himself concerning his ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vants <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">He will recal that severe sentence which for their sins he had passed upon them, and be reconciled to them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 115. 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11.</ns0:note> The idols of the heathen <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> silver and gold <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Of this and the following verses see the Notes on <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 115. 4, 5, &c.</ns0:note>, the work of mens hands.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 They have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 They have ears, but they hear not: nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther is there <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> breath in their mouths.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 They that make them <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>let them be.</ns0:hi> So Gr.</ns0:note> are like unto them: <ns0:hi>so is</ns0:hi> every one that trusteth in them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 Bless the LORD, O house of Israel: bless the LORD, O house of Aaron.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 Bless the LORD, O house of Levi: ye that fear the LORD, bless the LORD.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 Blessed be the LORD out of Zion <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">By the assemblies of his people in <ns0:hi>Zion</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Ierusalem.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, which dwelleth at Jerusalem <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">This clause may be added either to distinguish the true God from the gods which were worshipped in other places and countries; or as a reason why they should bless God, because he had blessed and honoured that place with his gra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cious and glorious presence.</ns0:note>.
